sanskrit: ओमित्येतदक्षरमुद्गीथमुपासीत । ओमिति ह्युद्गायति तस्योपव्याख्यानम्
transliteration: omityetadakṣaramudgīthamupāsīta | omiti hyudgāyati tasyopavyākhyānam
translation: Om is the closest word to Brahman . Recite this Om as if you are worshipping Brahman. [That is, treat this Om as the symbol of Brahman and concentrate on the idea of their oneness.] How you recite this Om is being explained.
word_meaning: Om iti, this Om [is closest to Brahman]; etat akṣaram udgītham upāsīta, recite this syllable as part of your upāsanā [ritual]; hi om iti udgāyati, how you recite this Om; tasya upavyākhyānam, is being explained.
commentary: Om is as good as Brahman. To begin with, it is a symbol of Brahman. But it is not just a symbol; it is Brahman itself. The Upaniṣad says to recite Om as if you are worshipping Brahman. This recitation is called udgītha, and it is loud recitation. You recite Om aloud, but you do it with the feeling that you are worshipping Brahman. This worship then eventually purifies the mind. The importance of Om is being explained in the following verses.
contextual_topics: The Individual Self Identical with the Infinite Brahman
claim_candidates: Reciting Om aloud with the conviction of worship constitutes a direct worship of Brahman
Om is not merely a symbol but is identical to Brahman
The proper vocalization (udgītha) of Om purifies the mind
Understanding the explanation of Om's recitation is essential for subsequent verses
objection_hooks: If Om is identical to Brahman, how can a sound be equated with the formless absolute?
The claim that vocal recitation purifies the mind may rely on psychological effects rather than metaphysical truth
Treating a symbolic syllable as Brahman could undermine the need for internal realization beyond external ritual

sanskrit: एषां भूतानां पृथिवी रसः पृथिव्या अपो रसः । अपामोषधयो रस ओषधीनां पुरुषो रसः पुरुषस्य वाग्रसो वाच ऋग्रस ऋचः साम रसः साम्न उद्गीथो रसः
transliteration: eṣāṃ bhūtānāṃ pṛthivī rasaḥ pṛthivyā apo rasaḥ | apāmoṣadhayo rasa oṣadhīnāṃ puruṣo rasaḥ puruṣasya vāgraso vāca ṛgrasa ṛcaḥ sāma rasaḥ sāmna udgītho rasaḥ
translation: The earth is the essence of all things, living or non-living; water is the essence of the earth; plants are the essence of water; human beings are the essence of plants; speech is the essence of human beings; the Ṛg Veda is the essence of speech; the Sāma Veda is the essence of the Ṛg Veda; and the udhītha is the essence of the Sāma Veda.
word_meaning: Eṣām bhūtānām, of these beings; pṛthivī rasaḥ, the earth is the essence; pṛthivyāḥ, of the earth; āpaḥ, water; rasaḥ, is the essence; apām oṣadhayaḥ rasaḥ, plants are the essence of water; oṣadhīnām puruṣaḥ rasaḥ, human beings are the essence of plants; puruṣasya vāk rasaḥ, speech is the essence of human beings; vācaḥ ṛg rasaḥ, the Ṛg Veda is the essence of speech; ṛcaḥ sāma rasaḥ, the Sāma Veda is the essence of the Ṛg Veda; sāmnaḥ udgīthaḥ rasaḥ, the part known as udgītha is the essence of the Sāma Veda.
commentary: There are both living and non-living things on the earth. What sustains them? Obviously the earth. They all come out of the earth, are sustained by the earth, and finally dissolve into the earth. But what sustains the earth? Water. The earth is a mixture of water and earth, and there can be no earth without water. Plants are said to be the essence of water, for they grow from water. Similarly, human beings are the essence of plants, because the human body is the outcome of the food eaten by human beings. Speech is the essence of human beings, for it is the best part of them. The best speech is the Ṛg Veda, and the essence of the Ṛg Veda is the Sāma Veda. Finally, udgītha—that is, Om—is the essence of the Sāma Veda.
claim_candidates: The earth functions as the foundational essence sustaining all beings, both animate and inanimate
Water is the essential principle that sustains the earth, implying a dependence of earth on water
Human speech, epitomized by the Rig Veda, is the essential expression of humanity, indicating that sacred texts embody the highest human faculty
The syllable Om (udhitha) represents the ultimate essence of the Vedic corpus, serving as the final substratum of all reality
The progressive chain of essences demonstrates a hierarchical cosmology where each higher level is the essential expression of the preceding lower level
objection_hooks: How can water be said to sustain the earth when geologically the earth contains water rather than being dependent on it
The identification of Om as the essence of the Sam Veda may be symbolic rather than ontological, questioning whether the claim asserts an ultimate reality or merely a ritual significance
The assertion that the Rig Veda is the essence of speech presumes a privileged status for one Veda over others, which could be challenged as sectarian bias rather than universal truth
The hierarchical chain may overlook the interdependence and cyclic nature of elements, reducing complex relationships to a linear order, which could be seen as an oversimplification

sanskrit: स एष रसानांरसतमः परमः परार्ध्योऽष्टमो यदुद्गीथः
transliteration: sa eṣa rasānāṃrasatamaḥ paramaḥ parārdhyo'ṣṭamo yadudgīthaḥ
translation: This udgītha [Om] is the best of all essences. It is the best of all that exists. It is the eighth, and it has the highest status.
word_meaning: Saḥ, that; eṣaḥ, this; rasānām, of all the essences; rasatamaḥ, the best essence; paramaḥ, the best; parārdhyaḥ, ranking the highest; aṣṭamaḥ, the eighth [in the order of earth, water, plants, human beings; speech, the Ṛg Veda, the Sāma Veda, and udgītha]; yāt, that; udgīthaḥ, udgītha [Om].
commentary: The best of all essences is the udgītha, which is Om. It is the highest and best because it is the same as Brahman .
claim_candidates: The udgītha (Om) constitutes the supreme essence among all existent essences
The udgītha holds the highest status among the eight enumerated categories
The udgītha is ontologically identical to Brahman
All other essences are subordinate to the udgītha because it is identified with Brahman
objection_hooks: How can a phonetic symbol like Om be regarded as the best of all essences when essences are usually understood as material or metaphysical entities
The verse calls the udgītha the eighth yet also the highest, creating a possible contradiction in ranking
The identification of Om with Brahman may be metaphorical; does the text provide sufficient justification for asserting ontological identity

sanskrit: कतमा कतमर्क्कतमत्कतमत्साम कतमः कतम उद्गीथ इति विमृष्टं भवति
transliteration: katamā katamarkkatamatkatamatsāma katamaḥ katama udgītha iti vimṛṣṭaṃ bhavati
translation: Which are the Ṛks? Which are the Sāmas ? Which are the udgīthas ? This is the question.
word_meaning: Katamā, which; katamā ṛk, which are the Ṛks; katamat katamat sāma, which are the Sāmas; katamaḥ katamaḥ udgīthaḥ, which are the udgīthas; iti vimṛṣṭam bhavati, this is the question.
commentary: It has been stated that speech is the essence of the Ṛg Veda . The question now arises: Which ones are the Ṛk, which ones are the Sāma, and which ones are the udgītha ? The word katama, ‘which, ’ is repeated to emphasize the importance of the question. But why is the word ‘which’ being used here? ‘Which’ is used when you have to pinpoint one thing out of many. The Ṛg Veda is taken as a single whole, so how is the use of ‘which’ justified here? The answer is that here ‘which’ refers to individual Ṛk mantras, and not to the whole body of the Ṛg Veda.
claim_candidates: The Rig Veda, though a single whole, is composed of individual mantras that can be distinctly identified as Ṛk, Sāma, or udgītha
The repeated use of the interrogative which indicates a methodological emphasis on precise classification within the Vedic corpus
Speech is considered the essential nature of the Rig Veda, implying that the Veda's authority derives from its verbal form
Identifying individual mantras is necessary for proper ritual application because each category serves distinct liturgical functions
objection_hooks: If the Rig Veda is a single whole, why is it necessary to isolate individual mantras; does this not fragment its unity
The claim that speech is the essence of the Rig Veda may be challenged by the view that the Veda's meaning lies in its underlying metaphysical truth rather than its phonetic expression
Emphasizing precise classification might be seen as a later scholastic addition, not an original intent of the seers; thus the methodological significance of which could be overstated

sanskrit: वागेवर्क्प्राणः सामोमित्येतदक्षरमुद्गीथः । तद्वा एतन्मिथुनं यद्वाक्च प्राणश्चर्क्च साम च
transliteration: vāgevarkprāṇaḥ sāmomityetadakṣaramudgīthaḥ | tadvā etanmithunaṃ yadvākca prāṇaścarkca sāma ca
translation: [In answer to the foregoing question: ] Speech is the same as Ṛk; prāṇa [life] is the same as Sāma; and Om is nothing but udgītha [ Brahman ] itself. They are pairs: speech and life, Ṛk and Sāma.
word_meaning: Vāk eva ṛk, speech is Ṛk [being the cause of the Ṛk]; prāṇaḥ sāma, prāṇa [breath, or the life force] is Sāma [for you can sing the Sāma if your prāṇa is strong]; om iti etat akṣaram udgīthaḥ, the syllable ‘Om’ is the udgītha [for you recite it out of love for the Sāma]; tat etat vai mithunam, it is like a couple; yat vāk ca prāṇaḥ ca ṛk ca sāma ca, which are speech and prāṇa, Ṛk and Sāma.
commentary: The word ‘couple, ’ or ‘pair, ’ is being used to suggest a relationship of cause and effect. Cause and effect are, in fact, one and the same. Speech is the cause, According to this Upaniṣad, the evolution of the gross world is in this order: earth, water, plants, human beings, speech, Ṛk, Sāma, and udgītha (Om). Udgītha is rasatamā, the essence of all essences, the cause of all causes. It occupies the eighth position—that is, it is the ultimate in the evolution of things. It is the Paramātman, the Self of all selves.
contextual_topics: The Individual Self Identical with the Infinite Brahman
The Unitary World-Self, The Immanent Reality of All Things and Man
claim_candidates: Speech (vāk) is ontologically identical to the sacrificial formula Ṛk, indicating that verbal expression manifests the sacred ritual principle
Prāṇa is equated with Sāma, suggesting that the life force is intrinsically linked to the melodic aspect of Vedic chant
The syllable Om is identified as udgītha, the essence of all essences and the cause of all causes, thereby claiming that Om is the ultimate Brahman itself

The commentary’s assertion that cause and effect are one and the same, illustrated by the pairings speech‑Ṛk and prāṇa‑Sāma, advances a doctrine that all dualities ultimately resolve into a single reality
The evolutionary sequence ending with udgītha (Om) as Paramātman implies that the highest stage of cosmic development is the realization of the universal Self
objection_hooks: The identification of Om with Brahman conflates a phonetic symbol with the ineffable absolute, raising the epistemic question of how a sound can fully represent the unconditioned reality
The claim that cause and effect are identical appears logically untenable, since causality traditionally presupposes a distinction between antecedent and consequent
The equation of prāṇa with Sāma may be a poetic analogy rather than a literal ontological identity, challenging the asserted unity of breath and sacred music
The evolutionary list may be metaphorical rather than a literal cosmological sequence, limiting the inference that the ultimate reality is reached only at the stage of Om

sanskrit: तदेतन्मिथुनमोमित्येतस्मिन्नक्षरे संसृज्यते यदा वै मिथुनौ समागच्छत आपयतो वै तावन्योन्यस्य कामम्
transliteration: tadetanmithunamomityetasminnakṣare saṃsṛjyate yadā vai mithunau samāgacchata āpayato vai tāvanyonyasya kāmam
translation: This dual combination of speech and life merge into each other and become one in this syllable Om. It is like a male and a female meeting and satisfying each other’s desires.
word_meaning: Tat, that; etat, this; mithunam, dual combination [i.e., speech and life]; om iti etasmin akṣare saṃsṛjyate, meet in this syllable Om; yadā vai, whenever; mithunau samāgacchataḥ, a couple [a male and a female] come together; tau, they; anyonyasya kāmam āpayataḥ vai, naturally satisfy each other’s desires.
commentary: Those two, speech and life, merge into each other in Om. They attain their fulfilment in this way. Om thus stands for the fulfilment of all things.
contextual_topics: The Unitary World-Self, The Immanent Reality of All Things and Man
claim_candidates: The syllable Om embodies the union of speech and life, indicating that ultimate reality transcends duality
In Om the male and female principles merge, suggesting that Brahman is the fulfillment of all desires
The merging of dualities in Om demonstrates that the apparent separation of phenomena is illusory
Om functions as a symbolic representation of the ultimate fulfillment of all things, implying that realization of Om leads to liberation
objection_hooks: If Om merely symbolizes the union of speech and life, how does it substantively affect the ontological status of Brahman beyond metaphor
The analogy of male and female may impose gendered dualism that contradicts the non‑dual claim of ultimate unity
The claim that realization of Om leads to liberation assumes a causal link not explicitly stated in the verse; the text only describes symbolic fulfillment

sanskrit: आपयिता ह वै कामानां भवति य एतदेवं विद्वानक्षरमुद्गीथमुपास्ते
transliteration: āpayitā ha vai kāmānāṃ bhavati ya etadevaṃ vidvānakṣaramudgīthamupāste
translation: He who worships Om as the udgītha [ Brahman ], knowing it as the one who receives everything, himself [finally] receives everything he desires. 20)
word_meaning: Āpayitā, he receives; ha vai kāmānām, all he desires; bhavati, this happens; yaḥ, he who; etat, this; evam, this way [as the one who receives everything]; vidvān, knows; akṣaram, Om; udgītham, as udgītha [Brahman]; upāste, worships.
commentary: If you worship Om, you acquire the qualities of Om. If you worship Om as the one who receives everything, you also, like Om, receive everything you desire. The śruti says: ‘You become whatever or whomever your object of worship is.’ ( Maṇḍala Brāhmaṇa
contextual_topics: The Individual Self Identical with the Infinite Brahman
claim_candidates: Worship of Om as the all‑receiving principle guarantees that the worshipper will obtain all his desires
The identity between the worshipper and the object of worship implies that the worshipper becomes identical with Brahman
Knowledge of Om as the immutable akṣara is a prerequisite for its efficacious worship
The efficacy of worship depends on the nature of the deity chosen, because one becomes whatever one worships
Om, being the receiver of everything, functions as a universal source of fulfillment for devotees
objection_hooks: If worship guarantees fulfillment of all desires, how does this reconcile with the law of karma that limits results of actions
Equating the worshipper with Brahman may ignore the ontological distinction between the individual self (jīva) and ultimate reality
The principle that one becomes whatever one worships seems problematic in a pluralistic context where multiple deities are worshipped; does the verse allow for contradictory outcomes

sanskrit: तद्वा एतदनुज्ञाक्षरं यद्धि किंचानुजानात्योमित्येव तदाहैषो एव समृद्धिर्यदनुज्ञा समर्धयिता ह वै कामानां भवति य एतदेवं विद्वानक्षरमुद्गीथमुपास्ते
transliteration: tadvā etadanujñākṣaraṃ yaddhi kiṃcānujānātyomityeva tadāhaiṣo eva samṛddhiryadanujñā samardhayitā ha vai kāmānāṃ bhavati ya etadevaṃ vidvānakṣaramudgīthamupāste
translation: That akṣaram [Om] stands for assent. A person says Om whenever he wants to say yes. This Om is the key to progress. He who worships Om as the udgītha [ Brahman ], knowing it thus [as the fulfiller of all desires], has all his desires fulfilled.
word_meaning: Tat, that; vai etat, this; anujñā akṣaram, syllable [Om] indicates assent; yat, when; hi kim ca anujānāti, assent is to be indicated; om iti, this Om; eva tadā āha, is then uttered; eṣā u eva, this; samṛddhiḥ, progress; yat, that; anujñā, assent; samardhayitā, makes it possible; ha vai kāmānām bhavati, one attains those desires; yaḥ, he who; etat, this; evam, this way; vidvān, having known; akṣaram udgītham upāste, worships the syllable Om as the udgītha [Brahman],
commentary: The word Om means ‘yes.’ Once someone named Śākalya asked the sage Yājñavalkya, ‘How many gods and goddesses are there?’ Yājñavalkya replied, ‘Thirty-three.’ Then Śākalya indicated his agreement by saying ‘Om.’ When you say Om it is also an indication of your faith in yourself. It is proof of your strength and vigour, and proof also of your prosperity. Om is therefore a symbol of certain basic qualities. When you worship Om you acquire those qualities, and you begin to progress and also prosper.
claim_candidates: Om functions as a verbal affirmation that signifies assent and agreement
Worship of Om as the udgītha (Brahman) leads to the fulfillment of all desires
The utterance of Om is a symbol of inner strength, vigor, and prosperity
Saying Om indicates faith in oneself
objection_hooks: The association of Om with desire fulfillment may be merely metaphorical, not a causal guarantee
Equating a simple syllable with inner strength could be seen as symbolic rhetoric lacking empirical evidence
Interpreting Om as an affirmation of self‑faith might ignore its broader ritual and communal functions

sanskrit: तेनेयं त्रयीविद्या वर्तते ओमित्याश्रावयत्योमिति शंसत्योमित्युद्गायत्येतस्यैवाक्षरस्यापचित्यै महिम्ना रसेन
transliteration: teneyaṃ trayīvidyā vartate omityāśrāvayatyomiti śaṃsatyomityudgāyatyetasyaivākṣarasyāpacityai mahimnā rasena
translation: With Om one begins the threefold Vedic ritual, and with Om one starts reciting the Vedas . With Om one starts singing the Vedic hymns, and again with Om one sings the udgān [from the Vedas, in praise of Om, or Brahman ]. All this is a tribute to Om. Again, all this is possible by virtue of the essence derived from Om [in the form of wheat and other food].
word_meaning: Tena, by this [Om]; iyam, this; trayī vidyā vartate, threefold Vedic ritual begins; om iti, with Om; āśrāvayati, the recitation begins; om iti śaṃsati, with Om begins the singing of the hymn; om iti udgāyati, with Om the udgān [the praise to Om] begins; etasya akṣarasya, to this akṣara [Brahman]; eva apacityai, to pay homage; mahimnā, for its greatness; rasena, with the essence [of Om],
commentary: To create some interest in Om, it is being praised here. Om is indispensable even if you are performing a Vedic ritual. You begin reciting a Vedic verse with Om, singing a Vedic hymn with Om, and closing your final udgān with Om. In short, the whole procedure is dedicated to Om. Not only that, those who participate in this ritualistic worship derive their strength and vigour from Om, for the butter or barley syrup they drink as a stimulant is from Om. How? Om is the medium through which sacrifices are performed, and the effects of the sacrifices are carried to the sun. These then return to the earth as rain. From rain come life and food. Again, because of life and food, a person is able to perform sacrifices. Thus, it is the essence of Om that makes ritualistic worship, such as sacrifices, possible. Ritualistic worship is therefore a testimony to the greatness of Om. Om is both the cause and the effect.
claim_candidates: Om is the indispensable medium through which all Vedic rituals are performed
The efficacy of sacrificial offerings, including the production of food and rain, ultimately depends on the essence of Om
Om functions both as the cause and the effect of ritualistic worship
The recitation, singing, and concluding udgān of Vedic hymns must begin with Om to honor its greatness
The physical sustenance consumed by participants, such as barley syrup, is derived from Om
objection_hooks: How can a phonetic syllable like Om be causally responsible for physical phenomena such as rain and food?
The assertion that Om is indispensable for rituals may overlook alternative ritual practices that do not invoke Om
Claiming Om is both cause and effect appears logically circular; does it not presuppose the very reality it seeks to prove?
The link between reciting Om and the efficacy of the ritual may be symbolic rather than literal, questioning the necessity implied

sanskrit: तेनोभौ कुरुतो यश्चैतदेवं वेद यश्च न वेद । नाना तु विद्या चाविद्या च यदेव विद्यया करोति श्रद्धयोपनिषदा तदेव वीर्यवत्तरं भवतीति खल्वेतस्यैवाक्षरस्योपव्याख्यानं भवति
transliteration: tenobhau kuruto yaścaitadevaṃ veda yaśca na veda | nānā tu vidyā cāvidyā ca yadeva vidyayā karoti śraddhayopaniṣadā tadeva vīryavattaraṃ bhavatīti khalvetasyaivākṣarasyopavyākhyānaṃ bhavati
translation: He who knows about Om and he who does not know about it both work with strength they derive from Om. But knowledge and ignorance produce different results. Anything done with knowledge [about Om], with faith in the teachers and in the scriptures, and according to the principles of the Upaniṣads [or of yoga ] is more fruitful. This certainly is the right tribute to Om.
word_meaning: Ubhau, both [kinds of persons]; tena, by the power of that [Om]; kurutaḥ, work; yaḥ ca, whoever; evam, as such; veda, knows; etat, this [i.e., about Om]; yaḥ ca na veda, he who does not know; vidyā ca avidyā ca nānā tu, knowledge and ignorance are entirely different things; yat eva, anything; vidyayā karoti, one does with knowledge [about Om]; śraddhayā, with respect for one’s teachers and the scriptures; upaniṣadā, as taught by the Upaniṣads [i.e., according to yoga]; tat eva, that [work]; vīryavattaram bhavati, . is more powerful [i.e., more fruitful]; iti, this; khalu, certainly; etasya eva akṣarasya upavyākhyānam bhavati, is the right tribute to this Om.
commentary: Two kinds of people work: one kind knowing what Om means and another kind knowing nothing about it. Both kinds of people, however, are able to work because of Om. What is the difference between the two? What special advantage does a person who knows about Om have? Someone may argue: Suppose a person takes a medicine knowing what medicine he is taking and why he is taking it, and another person takes it without any knowledge of what he is taking and why he is taking it. Will the medicine produce different results in them? The answer is: The analogy does not apply here. Knowledge is always an advantage, especially knowledge about Om. If you work because you are told to work, and if you work because you want to use the work as a stepping-stone to the attainment of Om—there is a vast difference between the two approaches. In the first instance, you are content with whatever the work produces; in the second, you are content only if it paves the way to your attainment of Om.
claim_candidates: Knowledge of Om confers greater efficacy to one’s actions than ignorance of Om
Both the knowledgeable and the ignorant derive their strength for work from Om
Faith in teachers and scriptures, aligned with Upaniṣadic principles, enhances the fruitfulness of actions performed with knowledge of Om
The proper tribute to Om is the explanation of its immutable (akṣara) nature
objection_hooks: How can we verify that knowledge of Om actually yields more fruitful results given the lack of empirical evidence
If both the knowledgeable and the ignorant draw strength from Om, why does the verse differentiate their outcomes
Does reliance on faith in teachers and scriptures undermine the claim that knowledge alone is sufficient for effective action
Is the notion of a ‘right tribute’ to Om as an explanation compatible with the idea that Om is beyond conceptualization

sanskrit: देवासुरा ह वै यत्र संयेतिरे उभये प्राजापत्यास्तद्ध देवा उद्गीथमाजह्रुरनेनैनानभिभविष्याम इति
transliteration: devāsurā ha vai yatra saṃyetire ubhaye prājāpatyāstaddha devā udgīthamājahruranenainānabhibhaviṣyāma iti
translation: The gods and goddesses and the demons are both children of Prajāpati, yet they fought among themselves. The gods and goddesses then adopted the path of the udgītha, thinking they would thereby be able to overcome the demons.
word_meaning: Devāsurāḥ . the gods and goddesses and the demons; ha vai yatra saṃyetire, fought among themselves; ubhaye, [though] both; prājāpatyāḥ, were Prajāpati’s children; tat, at that time; ha devāḥ, the gods and goddesses then; udgītham ājahruḥ, adopted the path of the udgītha; anena, by this; enān, them [the demons]; abhibhaviṣyāmah, will overcome; iti, thinking thus.
commentary: The gods and goddesses are ‘bright’ by virtue of their self-control, while the demons are ‘dark’ because they have no control over themselves. Though they were offspring of the same Prajāpati, they often clashed with each other. The gods and goddesses represent virtue; the demons represent vice. This conflict between virtue and vice is eternal, but it is virtue that always prevails. Virtue is here said to be the udgītha—that is, reciting Om while performing sacrifices. The gods and goddesses choose the path prescribed by the scriptures, whereas the demons do just the opposite and defy the scriptures. No wonder then the demons lose. The udgītha is supreme because it is Om. It is the Paramātman, the Cosmic Self.
contextual_topics: The Unitary World-Self, The Immanent Reality of All Things and Man
claim_candidates: Reciting Om (udgītha) while performing sacrifices guarantees victory over demonic forces
Both gods and demons originate from the same primordial source Prajāpati, indicating that moral distinction rests on self‑control rather than ontological difference
The sacred syllable Om is identical with the Paramātman, making it the ultimate means of liberation
Ethical self‑control is the essential quality that separates divine beings from demonic ones irrespective of their lineage
The conflict between virtue and vice is eternal, yet virtue inevitably prevails because it aligns with Om
objection_hooks: How can a mere vocal recitation of Om ensure overcoming external demonic forces; is there empirical support for this claim?
If gods and demons share the same origin, why does the text still assign them inherent moral categories?

sanskrit: ते ह नासिक्यं प्राणमुद्गीथमुपासांचक्रिरे तं हासुराः पाप्मना विविधुस्तस्मात्तेनोभयं जिघ्रति सुरभि च दुर्गन्धि च पाप्मना ह्येष विद्धः
transliteration: te ha nāsikyaṃ prāṇamudgīthamupāsāṃcakrire taṃ hāsurāḥ pāpmanā vividhustasmāttenobhayaṃ jighrati surabhi ca durgandhi ca pāpmanā hyeṣa viddhaḥ
translation: The gods and goddesses worshipped the prāṇa presiding over the nostrils as udgītha . The demons, however, misused it. [To them it was only an organ of smelling.] That is why [because of this misuse] people smell both good and bad odours through the nostrils.
word_meaning: Te, they [the gods and goddesses]; ha nāsikyam prāṇam udgītham upāsāñcakrire, worshipped as udgītha the prāṇa [life principle] presiding over the nostrils; asurāḥ ha, the asuras, however; tam pāpmanā vividhuḥ, pierced it with evil [i.e., misused it, as if it were meant only for sense pleasure such as enjoying fragrance]; hi, this is why; eṣaḥ, this [prāṇa presiding over the nostrils]; pāpmanā viddhaḥ, is tainted with evil; tasmāt, therefore; tena, by it [i.e., the nostrils]; jighrati, smells; surabhi ca, good odour; durgandhi ca, and also bad odour.
commentary: Mark the contrast between the attitude of the gods and goddesses and of the demons. To the demons, the nostrils were only an organ for smelling. The nostrils are also holy to them for another reason: they use the nostrils in reciting the udgītha to prāṇa. The demons know nothing about prāṇa or udgītha. To them, prāṇa is merely that which carries good and bad odours.

sanskrit: अथ ह वाचमुद्गीथमुपासांचक्रिरे तां हासुराः पाप्मना विविधुस्तस्मात्तयोभयं वदति सत्यं चानृतं च पाप्मना ह्येषा विद्धा

translation: Next, the gods and goddesses worshipped the mind, because the mind makes it possible for them to chant the udgītha [the praise to Om]. But the demons even vitiated the mind. As a result, the mind has both good and bad thoughts. This happens because of ignorance.

commentary: Prāṇa is another name for Brahman . Prāṇa is pure, but when it is associated with the sense organs it is not pure. Similarly, Brahman as Brahman is pure, but with adjuncts it is not pure. It is not pure in the sense that it is subject to change. Here, these adjuncts are referred to as pāpma, impure or evil, because they are limitations imposed on Brahman. These limitations are not real, however, but only apparent. When the Upaniṣad speaks of the organs, it means the organs with their presiding deities. Both are described as pāpma . In these verses, some of the organs are mentioned, but it is to be understood that what is stated here about some organs applies to all the organs and their presiding deities.

sanskrit: यथाश्मानमाखणमृत्वा विध्वंसत एवं हैव स विध्वंसते य एवंविदि पापं कामयते यश्चैनमभिदासति स एषोऽश्माखणः

translation: Just as when chunks of earth are thrown against an unbreakable stone they are themselves reduced to dust, similarly, if anyone wishes ill or causes an injury to a person who knows prāṇa, he invites his own destruction thereby. word_meaning: Evam yathā, just as [chunks of earth]; ākhaṇam, unbreakable; aśmānam, stone; ṛtvā, having hit; vidhvaṃsate, are smashed; evam ha eva, in the same way; saḥ vidhvaṃsate, a person gets totally destroyed; yaḥ pāpam kāmayate, who wishes ill; evamvidi, of a person who knows thus [the true nature of prāṇa]; yaḥ ca enam abhidāsati, or who causes an injury to such a person; saḥ eṣaḥ, he [who knows] this [prāṇa]; aśmā ākhaṇaḥ, [is like] a stone that can never be broken.

transliteration: tena taṃ ha bṛhaspatirudgīthamupāsāṃcakra etamu eva bṛhaspatiṃ manyante vāgghi bṛhatī tasyā eṣa patiḥ
translation: This is why Bṛhaspati worshipped prāṇa as udgītha . Prāṇa is regarded as Bṛhaspati, for vāk [speech] is great [ bṛhatī ] and prāṇa is its lord [ pati ].
word_meaning: Tena, for that reason; bṛhaspatiḥ, Bṛhaspati; ha tam, that [prāṇa]; udgītham upāsāñcakre, worshipped prāṇa as udgītha [as Brahman, to whom Om is sung]; etam u eva bṛhaspatim manyante, they regard this [prāṇa] as Bṛhaspati; hi, for; vāk, speech; bṛhatī, is powerful; tasyāḥ eṣaḥ patiḥ, prāṇa is its lord.
claim_candidates: Prāṇa is the ultimate lord of speech, indicating that breath underlies all verbal expression
Bṛhaspati, the deity of speech, is identified with prāṇa, equating the life‑force with the divine source of wisdom
Worship of prāṇa as udgītha treats the breath as a representation of Brahman that is sung in the sacred syllable Om
The greatness of vāk (speech) is derived from its dependence on prāṇa, so without breath speech cannot manifest
objection_hooks: If prāṇa is merely a subtle physiological principle, how can it be equated with a deity such as Bṛhaspati
Equating speech’s greatness solely to its dependence on breath may reduce the sacred status of vāk to a mere byproduct
The term udgītha might refer to a specific mantra rather than the totality of Brahman, challenging the claim that prāṇa is worshipped as Brahman

sanskrit: तेन तं हायास्य उद्गीथमुपासांचक्र एतमु एवायास्यं मन्यन्त आस्याद्यदयते
transliteration: tena taṃ hāyāsya udgīthamupāsāṃcakra etamu evāyāsyaṃ manyanta āsyādyadayate
translation: This is why Āyāsya worshipped prāṇa as udgītha . They regarded this as Āyāsya for it is that which comes [ayate] out of the mouth [āsyāt] .
word_meaning: Tena, for that reason; tam, that [i.e., the chief prāṇa]; ha āyāsya, the sage Āyāsya [or, that which comes out of the mouth]; udgītham, as udgītha; upāsāñcakre, worshipped; etam u eva āyāsyam manyante, they regarded this as Āyāsya; yat āsyāt ayate, that which comes out of the mouth.
commentary: Prāṇa is also Bṛhaspati because it is the lord of all speech. Āyāsya means ‘that which comes out of the mouth.’ It is prāṇa, but it is also the name of a sage. Aṅgirā, Bṛhaspati, and Āyāsya—these sages worshipped prāṇa as udgītha. They, in fact, worshipped themselves.
contextual_topics: The Individual Self Identical with the Infinite Brahman
claim_candidates: Worship of prāṇa as udgītha constitutes worship of the self, implying that the self is identical with the life‑breath
Prāṇa, as the lord of all speech, functions as a symbolic representation of Brahman, linking breath to the ultimate reality
The identification of Āyāsya with that which comes out of the mouth suggests that ultimate knowledge is expressed through speech rather than solely through silent contemplation
The act of worshipping prāṇa by sages indicates that external ritual is unnecessary when one recognizes the inner prāṇa as Brahman
The equivalence of prāṇa, Bṛhaspati, and the sage Āyāsya demonstrates that the divine principle pervades both the cosmic order and individual consciousness
objection_hooks: How can worship of a physiological process like breath be equated with worship of the self without conflating metaphor with ontology
The identification of prāṇa with Brahman may overlook the distinction between the material breath and the transcendent absolute, leading to logical inconsistency
Asserting that speech is the sole medium of ultimate knowledge discounts the role of silent meditation emphasized elsewhere in the Upanishads
Claiming external rituals are unnecessary may conflict with scriptural injunctions that prescribe specific rites for purification

sanskrit: तेन तंह बको दाल्भ्यो विदांचकार । स ह नैमिशीयानामुद्गाता बभूव स ह स्मैभ्यः कामानागायति
transliteration: tena taṃha bako dālbhyo vidāṃcakāra | sa ha naimiśīyānāmudgātā babhūva sa ha smaibhyaḥ kāmānāgāyati
translation: The sage Baka, son of Dalbha, came to know prāṇa as it was. That is why the sages of Naimiṣa forest selected him as the singer of their udgītha . He, in his turn, fulfilled their wishes.
word_meaning: Dālbhyaḥ, the son of Dalbha; bakaḥ, the sage Baka; ha tam, that [prāṇa]; tena, with the qualities as stated; vidāñcakāra, came to know; saḥ, he [Baka]; ha naimiṣīyānām, of the sages of Naimiṣa forest; udgātā, the singer of the udgītha; babhūva, became; ha ebhyaḥ kāmān, according to the wishes [of the forest dwellers]; saḥ āgāyati sma, he sang [the udgītha].
commentary: Not only did Aṅgirā and other sages worship prāṇa, but Baka, son of Dalbha, also did the same. That is, he recognized the power of prāṇa. The sages of Naimiṣa forest were pleased with him, and appointed him to sing the udgītha for them. He thus sang the udgītha in praise of prāṇa and pleased the sages by his performance.
contextual_topics: Being as the Source of All
The Unitary World-Self, The Immanent Reality of All Things and Man
claim_candidates: The recognition of prāṇa as it truly is constitutes knowledge of the ultimate reality
The appointment of Baka as the udgītha singer shows that praising prāṇa through song is an accepted means of honoring the divine
The fulfillment of the sages' wishes by Baka indicates that alignment with prāṇa leads to the granting of desires
The reverence of multiple sages for prāṇa suggests a consensus on its supreme status within Vedic tradition
objection_hooks: The knowledge of prāṇa may be a partial insight and not equivalent to knowledge of Brahman
Singing may complement but not replace traditional ritual sacrifices in honoring the divine
The correlation between spiritual insight and wish fulfillment could be coincidental rather than causal
The text mentions only a few sages, so claiming a broad consensus on prāṇa's status may be overstated

sanskrit: आगाता ह वै कामानां भवति य एतदेवं विद्वानक्षरमुद्गीथमुपास्त इत्यध्यात्मम्
transliteration: āgātā ha vai kāmānāṃ bhavati ya etadevaṃ vidvānakṣaramudgīthamupāsta ityadhyātmam
translation: If a person knows the real meaning of prāṇa and worships it as udgītha akṣara [i.e., as Akṣara Brahman ] he himself becomes Akṣara Brahman. He then worships everyone he wants to worship [i.e., in singing for prāṇa he sings for all], and he attains all he desires. This is the attainment on the level of the body [ adhyātma ] . [The inner attainment is that he becomes one with prāṇa—that is, Akṣara Brahman.]
word_meaning: Yaḥ, he who; evam, as such; vidvān, knows; ; etat, this [prāṇa]; udgītham akṣaram, as udgītha akṣara [akṣara means both ‘syllable’ and ‘the undecaying, ’ which is a name of Brahman]; upāste, worships [or meditates on]; vai kāmānām āgātā ha bhavati, he thereby becomes the udgātā [singer] of all that he desires; iti adhyātmam, this is so far as the udgītha relating to the body is concerned.
commentary: Singing for prāṇa is the same as singing for all, for prāṇa is all. You may even achieve all you desire through it. This is so far as the individual is concerned. Praising Om has a threefold reward: relating to the body ( adhyātma ), relating to animals ( adhibhūta ), and relating to the elements ( adhidaiva ).
contextual_topics: The Individual Self Identical with the Infinite Brahman
claim_candidates: He who knows the true nature of prāṇa and worships it as the imperishable syllable becomes the imperishable Brahman
Worship of prāṇa as udgītha akṣara enables one to attain any desire because singing for prāṇa is equivalent to singing for all
The attainment described is limited to the bodily (adhyātma) level, indicating an inner bodily realization rather than supra‑physical liberation
Praising Om, which is equated with singing for prāṇa, yields threefold rewards concerning the body, animals, and elements
The term akṣara functions both as a linguistic symbol and as a name of the eternal Brahman, showing a symbolic representation of ultimate reality
objection_hooks: How can mere knowledge and worship transform a finite individual into the infinite Brahman
Does attaining all desires through worship of prāṇa contradict the Upanishadic emphasis on detachment
The commentary mentions threefold reward for praising Om, but the verse only discusses bodily attainment; is the extension justified
If the transformation is only at the bodily level, can it truly be equated with becoming the imperishable Brahman

sanskrit: अथाधिदैवतं य एवासौ तपति तमुद्गीथमुपासीतोद्यन्वा एष प्रजाभ्य उद्गायति । उद्यंस्तमो भयमपहन्त्यपहन्ता ह वै भयस्य तमसो भवति य एवं वेद
transliteration: athādhidaivataṃ ya evāsau tapati tamudgīthamupāsītodyanvā eṣa prajābhya udgāyati | udyaṃstamo bhayamapahantyapahantā ha vai bhayasya tamaso bhavati ya evaṃ veda
translation: Next, how you worship from the standpoint of the forces of nature: There is the sun rising to give us heat. Worship it as udgītha . The sun rises to pray, as it were, for the welfare of all living beings. As it rises, it dispels the fear of darkness. One who knows this overcomes the fear of ignorance about birth and death.
word_meaning: Atha, next; adhidaivatam, relating to the elements [such as rain, lightning, and other forces of nature]; yaḥ eva asau, that [i.e., the sun] over there which; tapati, gives us heat; tam, to that; udgītham upāsīta, worship as udgītha; udyan, as it rises; vai eṣaḥ, this [sun]; prajābhyaḥ, for all living beings; udgāyati, [as if] it prays for their well-being; udyan, as [the sun] rises; tamaḥ bhayam apahanti, it removes the fear of darkness; yaḥ, one who; evam veda, knows this; vai bhayasya, the fear [of birth and death]; tamasaḥ, ignorance; apahantā bhavati, overcomes.
commentary: There are many ways of using udgītha as worship. This verse gives an example of how you use it in worshipping the forces of nature ( adhidaivata ). There is the sun above giving us heat. The Upaniṣad says to worship udgītha as the sun. But if udgītha is Om, how can it stand for the sun? The sun helps the plants, such as paddy, to grow. Without the sun, life on this planet would be impossible. It is as if the sun sings the udgītha for us to sustain us. This is why the sun is referred to as the udgītha. As udgītha, the sun also dispels our fear of darkness. One who knows this is no longer afraid of birth and death. That is, he knows he is immortal.
contextual_topics: The Individual Self Identical with the Infinite Brahman
Brahman as Life, Joy, and the Void
claim_candidates: Worshiping the sun as udgītha equates a natural phenomenon with the sacred syllable Om
The rising sun dispels the fear of darkness, symbolizing the removal of ignorance about birth and death
Knowing the sun’s role as udgītha leads to liberation from the fear of mortality
The sun, as a manifestation of adhidaivata, serves as a substitute for ritual worship of the divine
Identifying the sun with udgītha implies that the ultimate reality can be realized through observation of natural processes
objection_hooks: The equation of the sun with Om may be metaphorical rather than ontological, so the claim of equivalence is questionable
Dispelling physical darkness does not necessarily remove metaphysical ignorance about birth and death; the connection may be symbolic
Knowing the sun’s role does not guarantee liberation; deeper inner practice may be required beyond external observation
Using natural phenomena as substitutes for ritual could undermine the prescribed Vedic sacrificial system
The claim that observation of the sun yields realization of Brahman may overlook the need for meditative insight

sanskrit: समान उ एवायं चासौ चोष्णोऽयमुष्णोऽसौ स्वर इतीममाचक्षते स्वर इति प्रत्यास्वर इत्यमुं तस्माद्वा एतमिमममुं चोद्गीथमुपासीत
transliteration: samāna u evāyaṃ cāsau coṣṇo'yamuṣṇo'sau svara itīmamācakṣate svara iti pratyāsvara ityamuṃ tasmādvā etamimamamuṃ codgīthamupāsīta
translation: This prāṇa and that sun are alike. Prāṇa is warm, and the sun is also warm. Prāṇa is called svara [when it is ‘going out’ at the time of death]. The sun is also described as svara [when it ‘sets’] and pratyāsvara [when it ‘comes back’]. Therefore, worship both prāṇa and the sun as udgītha .
word_meaning: Ayam, this [prāṇa]; ca asau, and that [sun]; samānaḥ eva, are equivalent; u ayam, this [prāṇa]; uṣṇaḥ, is warm; ca asau, and that [sun]; uṣṇaḥ, is warm; imam, this [prāṇa]; svaraḥ iti ācakṣate, [sages] call it svara [‘outgoing, ’ at the time of death]; amum, that [sun]; svaraḥ iti, has set; pratyāsvaraḥ iti, [and] has returned [this is what people say]; tasmāt vai, for that reason; etam, this [going out]; imam, this [prāṇa]; ca amum, and that [sun]; udgītham upāsīta, worship as udgītha.
commentary: Prāṇa and āditya (the sun) are similar. Both are warm. Sages call both svara, which means ‘going out.’ The difference is that while prāṇa goes out (at the time of death), the sun goes out (when it sets) and also returns ( pratyāsvara, when it rises). Thus, prāṇa and āditya are similar in name and quality. It is therefore appropriate to worship both as udgītha. Both are Om.
claim_candidates: The prāṇa and the sun are ontologically equivalent because both are warm and called svara
The term svara signifies a process of going out that applies both to the breath at death and to the sun at sunset
Worship of prāṇa and the sun as udgītha is justified by their shared identity as Om
Since the sun returns (pratyāsvara) while prāṇa does not, worship of both acknowledges both permanence and transience in the divine
objection_hooks: Equating prāṇa with the sun conflates an internal subtle principle with a physical celestial body, creating a category error
Interpreting svara solely as going out ignores other scriptural meanings of svara such as sound, weakening the exclusive application claim
Claiming that worship of prāṇa and the sun as udgītha is justified by their identity as Om presumes a metaphysical equation not explicitly stated in the verse
Reading the observation of the sun’s rise and fall as a doctrine of permanence and transience may overextend the simple textual description

sanskrit: अथ खलु व्यानमेवोद्गीथमुपासीत यद्वै प्राणिति स प्राणो यदपानिति सोऽपानः । अथ यः प्राणापानयोः संधिः स व्यानो यो व्यानः सा वाक् । तस्मादप्राणन्ननपानन्वाचमभिव्याहरति
transliteration: atha khalu vyānamevodgīthamupāsīta yadvai prāṇiti sa prāṇo yadapāniti so'pānaḥ | atha yaḥ prāṇāpānayoḥ saṃdhiḥ sa vyāno yo vyānaḥ sā vāk | tasmādaprāṇannanapānanvācamabhivyāharati
translation: Worship vyāna [the breath held between prāṇa and apāna that enables you to speak] as udgītha . Prāṇa is the breath drawn in and apāna is the breath drawn out. Vyāna is the breath held between prāṇa and apāna. This vyāna is also called vāk [speech], for in speaking a person has to hold the breath.
word_meaning: Atha, indirectly; khalu vyānam eva udgītham upāsīta, one should worship vyāna [the bridge between prāṇa (breathing in) and apāna (breathing out)] as udgītha; yat vai prāṇiti, that which is breathed in; saḥ prāṇaḥ, that is prāṇa; yat apāniti, that which is breathed out; saḥ apānaḥ, that is apāna; atha yat prāṇa-apānayoḥ sandhiḥ, then the bridge between prāṇa and apāna; saḥ vyānaḥ, that is vyāna; yaḥ vyānaḥ sā vāk, that which is vyāna is speech; tasmāt, therefore; aprāṇan, without inhaling; anapānan, without exhaling; vācam abhivyāharati, a person speaks.
commentary: Here vyāna is being presented for worship as udgītha, for vyāna is only a form of prāṇa. What is vyāna? Vyāna is the bridge between prāṇa and apāna, between breathing in and breathing out. Vyāna is the state in which you hold your breath. Vyāna is also called vāk, speech, for when you speak you have to hold your breath. Śaṅkara says prāṇa is breathing out and apāna is breathing in. According to Monier-Williams, it is the other way around—prāṇa is breathing in and apāna is breathing out. Macdowell is of the same opinion. Both meanings are correct, depending on the context in which the word is used.
claim_candidates: Vyāna, the breath held between prāṇa and apāna, is worthy of worship as udgītha
Speech vāk is fundamentally dependent on the retention of breath known as vyāna
The bridge sandhi between inhalation prāṇa and exhalation apāna constitutes the essential function of vyāna
Absence of inhalation aprāṇa and exhalation anapāna precludes the expression of speech
objection_hooks: If vyāna is merely a physiological process, can it truly be an object of worship or does worship require a transcendent entity
The dependence of speech on breath may be a functional description, not implying that breath is the ultimate cause of verbal expression; could speech arise from mental intention independent of breath
Identifying the bridge between prāṇa and apāna as the essential function of vyāna might overlook other roles of prāṇa in subtle physiology; is this reductionist
The claim that without inhalation and exhalation speech cannot occur assumes a strict physicalist view; could silent speech or internal thought be considered speech without breath

sanskrit: या वाक्सर्क्तस्मादप्राणन्ननपानन्नृचमभिव्याहरति यर्क्तत्साम तस्मादप्राणन्ननपानन्साम गायति यत्साम स उद्गीथस्तस्मादप्राणन्ननपानन्नुद्गायति
transliteration: yā vāksarktasmādaprāṇannanapānannṛcamabhivyāharati yarktatsāma tasmādaprāṇannanapānansāma gāyati yatsāma sa udgīthastasmādaprāṇannanapānannudgāyati
translation: Whatever is vāk [speech] is also the Ṛk [part of the Ṛg Veda ]. This is why a person stops breathing in and breathing out when reciting the Ṛk mantras . Whatever is the Ṛk is also the Sāma . This is why one recites the Sāma without breathing in or breathing out. That which is the Sāma is also the udgītha . This is why when one sings the udgītha one stops both breathing in and breathing out.
word_meaning: Yā vāk sā ṛk, that which is speech is Ṛk; tasmāt, because [they are one]; aprāṇan anapānan, breathing in and out are suspended; ṛcam, the Ṛg Veda; abhivyāharati, one recites; yā ṛk tat sāma, that which is the Ṛk is also the Sāma; tasmāt, because [they are one and the same]; aprāṇan anapānan sāma gāyati, one suspends breathing in and out when singing the Sāma; yat sāma saḥ udgīthaḥ, that which is the Sāma is the udgītha; tasmāt aprāṇan anapānan udgāyati, because one sings the udgītha by suspending both breathing in and breathing out.
commentary: The Ṛk is a collection of words, and the Sāma is based on the Ṛk. Again, the Sāma and the udgītha are the same. To recite any of these, or even to speak, you have to resort to vyāna —that is, you must hold your breath.
contextual_topics: The Unitary World-Self, The Immanent Reality of All Things and Man
claim_candidates: The verse asserts that speech (vāk) is ontologically identical to the Ṛk portion of the Ṛg Veda
Because of this identity the practitioner must suspend inhalation and exhalation while reciting the Ṛk indicating that true recitation transcends ordinary breath
The text equates the Ṛk with the Sāma and the Sāma with the udgītha presenting a single unified Vedic mode of expression
The repeated requirement to hold the breath for Ṛk Sāma and udgītha implies that their ultimate reality lies beyond the physical body suggesting a metaphysical unity of sound and consciousness
objection_hooks: How can any speech be identical to the specific hymns of the Ṛk if speech includes innumerable utterances beyond the Vedic corpus
Does the instruction to stop breathing refer to a literal physiological breath‑hold or is it a metaphor for mental concentration during chanting
If the Ṛk Sāma and udgītha are the same why does the tradition maintain separate musical and ritual classifications for them
Could the breath‑suspension rule be a practical technique for proper pronunciation rather than an ontological claim about the nature of the chants

sanskrit: अतो यान्यन्यानि वीर्यवन्ति कर्माणि यथाग्नेर्मन्थनमाजेः सरणं दृढस्य धनुष आयमनमप्राणन्ननपानंस्तानि करोत्येतस्य हेतोर्व्यानमेवोद्गीथमुपासीत
transliteration: ato yānyanyāni vīryavanti karmāṇi yathāgnermanthanamājeḥ saraṇaṃ dṛḍhasya dhanuṣa āyamanamaprāṇannanapānaṃstāni karotyetasya hetorvyānamevodgīthamupāsīta
translation: This is why, while doing feats demanding great strength—such as producing a fire by rubbing one stick of wood against another, running up to a target, or bending a stiff bow—a person does not breathe in or breathe out. For this reason, one should worship this holding of breath, called vyāna, as udgītha [Om].
word_meaning: Ataḥ, this is why; yāni, those; anyāni, other; vīryavanti, demanding great strength; karmāṇi, feats; yathā, such as; agneḥ manthanam, igniting a fire by rubbing one piece of wood against another; ājeh, a target; saraṇam, running up to; dṛḍhasya dhanuṣaḥ āyamanam, bending a stiff bow; aprāṇan anapānan, without breathing in or breathing out; tāni, all those [feats]; karoti, one accomplishes; etasya hetoḥ, for this reason; vyānam eva, vyāna; udgītham, as udgītha [Om]; upāsīta, one should worship.
commentary: Whenever you do something that demands much application of strength, you must resort to vyāna. Take, for instance, deeds such as producing fire by grinding one piece of wood against another, or running up to a target, or bending a stiff bow. In doing each of these feats, you have to hold your breath. Even when you speak, you hold your breath. This distinguishes vyāna from other forms of breathing. Vyāna, therefore, deserves special worship, for vyāna is in a class by itself. It gives you strength.
claim_candidates: Holding the breath (vyāna) during strenuous actions is a form of worship equivalent to chanting Om
The practice of breath retention (vyāna) confers strength to the practitioner
Vyāna is distinct from ordinary breathing and thus merits a unique devotional status
The omission of inhalation and exhalation during effort indicates a deeper connection to the sacred syllable Om
objection_hooks: How can a physical act like breath-holding be ontologically equivalent to the utterance of a sacred sound
Does breath retention truly generate strength, or is the perceived strength merely a physiological response
If vyāna is a substitute for Om, does this diminish the importance of vocal recitation in Vedic practice

sanskrit: अथ खलूद्गीथाक्षराण्युपासीतोद्गीथ इति प्राण एवोत्प्राणेन ह्युत्तिष्ठति वाग्गीर्वाचो ह गिर इत्याचक्षतेऽन्नं थमन्ने हीदंसर्वंस्थितम्
transliteration: atha khalūdgīthākṣarāṇyupāsītodgītha iti prāṇa evotprāṇena hyuttiṣṭhati vāggīrvāco ha gira ityācakṣate'nnaṃ thamanne hīdaṃsarvaṃsthitam
translation: Now, one should worship the syllables ut, gī and tha separately in the word udgītha . Prāṇa is represented by ut, for prāṇa is responsible for the
word_meaning: Atha, now; khalu udgīthākṣarāṇi ‘ut-gī-tha’ iti upāsīta, worship the syllables ut, gī, and tha separately in the word udgītha; prāṇaḥ eva ut, prāṇa is this ut; prāṇena hi, because by prāṇa; uttiṣṭhati, arises [everything]; vāk gīḥ, vāk [speech] is gī; vācaḥ ha giraḥ iti ācakṣate, because words are called ‘ gira ’; annam tham, food is tha; hi idam sarvam, for all this [i.e., this world]; anne sthitam, is supported by food.
commentary: The word udgītha is comprised of the syllables ut, gī, and tha . It is worthwhile meditating on these syllables, for each one is significant. For instance, ut, in brief, is uttham, rising. It stands for prāṇa, because out of prāṇa everything comes into being. From prāṇa everything ‘rises’; otherwise it goes down. The syllable gī stands for speech, because scholars prefer to use the word gira to mean speech. Similarly, the syllable tha stands for food, for tha means ‘that which supports.’ It is well known that food supports everything. Thus the syllables ut, gī, and tha stand for the whole word udgītha . It is like thinking of the name ‘Ram Misra .’ As you think of the name, you also think of the person who bears that name. Try to think of each syllable in the word udgītha as above.
contextual_topics: Brahman as Life, Joy, and the Void
claim_candidates: The syllable ut, identified with prāṇa, is portrayed as the origin from which all phenomena arise
The syllable gī, identified with speech, is presented as a divine expression linking language to the ultimate reality
The syllable tha, identified with food, is described as the essential support sustaining the entire world
Contemplating the individual syllables of a word is advocated as a legitimate means of spiritual realization

sanskrit: द्यौरेवोदन्तरिक्षं गीः पृथिवी थमादित्य एवोद्वायुर्गीरग्निस्थं सामवेद एवोद्यजुर्वेदो गीरृग्वेदस्थं दुग्धेऽस्मै वाग्दोहं यो वाचो दोहोऽन्नवानन्नादो भवति य एतान्येवं विद्वानुद्गीथाक्षराण्युपास्त उद्गीथ इति
transliteration: dyaurevodantarikṣaṃ gīḥ pṛthivī thamāditya evodvāyurgīragnisthaṃ sāmaveda evodyajurvedo gīrṛgvedasthaṃ dugdhe'smai vāgdohaṃ yo vāco doho'nnavānannādo bhavati ya etānyevaṃ vidvānudgīthākṣarāṇyupāsta udgītha iti
translation: Heaven is ut, the space between heaven and the earth is gī, and the earth is tha . The sun is ut, air is gī, and fire is tha . The Sāma Veda is ut, the Yajur Veda is gī, and the Ṛg Veda is tha . The scriptures reveal their meaning to the seeker if he knows all this. One who worships ut-gī-tha as above gets plenty of food and also eats plenty of food. [Such a person also gets enlightenment.]
word_meaning: Dyauḥ, heaven; eva ut, is ut; antarikṣam gīḥ, the space between heaven and earth is gī; pṛthivī tham, the earth is tha; ādityaḥ eva ut, the sun is ut; vāyuḥ gīḥ, air is gī; agniḥ tham, fire is tha; sāma vedaḥ eva ut, the Sāma Veda is ut; yajur vedaḥ gīḥ, the Yajur Veda is gī; ṛg vedaḥ tham, the Ṛg Veda is tha; vāk, the Ṛg Veda and other scriptures; asmai, to him [the spiritual seeker]; doham, the goal [he is seeking]; dugdhe, gives him of itself; yaḥ vācaḥ dohaḥ, the goal is the knowledge of the scriptures; yaḥ evam vidvān, the seeker who knows this; etāni udgīthākṣarāṇi ut + gī + tha iti upāste, [and] worships these syllables of udgītha; annavān, he has plenty of food; annādaḥ bhavati, [and] he enjoys eating that food [i.e., he becomes illumined].
commentary: Heaven is said to be ut because it is high above. Space is gī because it envelops the whole world. And the earth is tha because it is the support of all beings. Āditya, the sun, is ut because it is far above everything. Vāyu, air, is gī because it envelops everything. Agni, fire, is tha because it is the common element in every sacrificial rite. The Sāma Veda is said to be ut because it is known even in heaven. The Yajur Veda is gī because the butter used in performing the Yajur Vedic rites is eaten by the gods and goddesses. The Ṛg Veda is tha because it supports the Sāma Veda. What do you gain by worshipping ut-gī-tha ? You gradually understand the meaning of the Ṛg Veda and other Vedas . You also have plenty to eat, and you become like ‘a blazing fire’—that is, you become an illumined person.
contextual_topics: The Individual Self Identical with the Infinite Brahman

sanskrit: अथ खल्वाशीःसमृद्धिरुपसरणानीत्युपासीत येन साम्ना स्तोष्यन्स्यात्तत्सामोपधावेत्

sanskrit: येन च्छन्दसा स्तोष्यन्स्यात्तच्छन्द उपधावेद्येन स्तोमेन स्तोष्यमाणः स्यात्तंस्तोममुपधावेत्

sanskrit: यां दिशमभिष्टोष्यन्स्यात्तां दिशमुपधावेत्

sanskrit: आत्मानमन्तत उपसृत्य स्तुवीत कामं ध्यायन्नप्रमत्तोऽभ्याशो ह यदस्मै स कामः समृध्येत यत्कामः स्तुवीतेति यत्कामः स्तुवीतेति

sanskrit: अथ खलु य उद्गीथः स प्रणवो यः प्रणवः स उद्गीथ इत्यसौ वा आदित्य उद्गीथ एष प्रणव ओमिति ह्येष स्वरन्नेति
transliteration: atha khalu ya udgīthaḥ sa praṇavo yaḥ praṇavaḥ sa udgītha ityasau vā āditya udgītha eṣa praṇava omiti hyeṣa svaranneti
translation: That which is udgītha is also praṇava [Om]. So also, that which is praṇava is udgītha. That sun is udgītha, and it is also praṇava, because it seems to say Om [or, has the word Om in its mind] when it appears.
word_meaning: Atha, next; yaḥ khalu udgīthaḥ, that which is udgītha; saḥ praṇavaḥ, is praṇava [Om]; yaḥ praṇavaḥ saḥ udgīthaḥ, that which is praṇava is also udgītha; asau vai ādityaḥ udgīthaḥ, that sun is udgītha; eṣaḥ praṇavaḥ, it is also praṇava; hi, for; eṣaḥ, the sun; om iti svaran eti, appears with the word Om in its mind.
commentary: This is how udgītha is to be worshipped: According to many scholars of the Ṛg Veda, udgītha is the same as praṇava (Om). What is praṇava to them is udgītha according to the Chāndogya. Similarly, according to many scholars, the sun is udgītha and also praṇava. How can the sun be referred to as udgītha ? When the sun appears, it looks as if it is saying Om, or it has Om in its thoughts. According to Śaṅkara, the word svaran may also mean ‘uttering.’
sub_concepts: Brahman as Cosmological and Physical Principle

sanskrit: एतमु एवाहमभ्यगासिषं तस्मान्मम त्वमेकोऽसीति ह कौषीतकिः पुत्रमुवाच रश्मींस्त्वं पर्यावर्तयाद्बहवो वै ते भविष्यन्तीत्यधिदैवतम्
transliteration: etamu evāhamabhyagāsiṣaṃ tasmānmama tvameko'sīti ha kauṣītakiḥ putramuvāca raśmīṃstvaṃ paryāvartayādbahavo vai te bhaviṣyantītyadhidaivatam
translation: The sage Kauṣītaki said to his son: ‘I worshipped the sun and its rays as one. That is why I had only one son, which is you. If you worship the sun and its rays separately, you will then have many children.’ This is the worship of the forces of nature.
word_meaning: Kauṣītakiḥ putram uvāca, the sage Kauṣītaki said to his son; etam, this [sun with its rays]; eva, as one; aham abhyagāsiṣam, I greeted [welcomed]; tasmāt, because [of my worshipping it as one]; tvam mama ekaḥ asi, you are my only son; tvam raśmīn paryāvartayāt, if you worship the sun and its rays separately; te bahavaḥ vai bhaviṣyanti, you will have many children; iti adhidaivatam, this is the worship of the forces of nature.
contextual_topics: Man’s Destiny Determined by His Conduct
sub_concepts: Brahman as Cosmological and Physical Principle

Distinguishing between the sun and its rays in worship leads to an increase in offspring

sanskrit: अथाध्यात्मं य एवायं मुख्यः प्राणस्तमुद्गीथमुपासीतोमिति ह्येष स्वरन्नेति
transliteration: athādhyātmaṃ ya evāyaṃ mukhyaḥ prāṇastamudgīthamupāsītomiti hyeṣa svaranneti
translation: Next, this is how worship concerning the physical body is performed: One should worship the chief prāṇa as udgītha, for it seems to say Om as it makes the organs [of perception and action] function.
word_meaning: Atha, now; adhyātmam, concerning one’s own body; yaḥ eva ayam mukhyaḥ prāṇaḥ, that which is the chief prāṇa [which divides itself into five functions: prāṇa, apāna, vyāna, udāna, and samāna ]; tam udgītham upāsīta, one should worship as udgītha; hi, for; eṣaḥ, this [prāṇa]; om iti svaran, uttering Om; eti, activates [all the organs—of speech, vision, etc.].
commentary: As far as the physical body is concerned, the Upaniṣad says to treat the chief prāna as Om. The chief prāṇa is responsible for what the organs of perception (the eyes, ears, nose, etc.) and the organs of action (the hands, feet, speech, etc.) do. It makes them active. Just as some people say Om before they do or say anything, so prāṇa seems to say Om as it makes the organs function. Not that it really says Om, but because the organs cannot act without its support, it is suggested that the chief prāṇa has to give the signal (that is, by saying Om) and then only do the organs start operating.
contextual_topics: The Individual Self Identical with the Infinite Brahman

sanskrit: एतमु एवाहमभ्यगासिषं तस्मान्मम त्वमेकोऽसीति ह कौषीतकिः पुत्रमुवाच प्राणांस्त्वं भूमानमभिगायताद्बहवो वै मे भविष्यन्तीति
transliteration: etamu evāhamabhyagāsiṣaṃ tasmānmama tvameko'sīti ha kauṣītakiḥ putramuvāca prāṇāṃstvaṃ bhūmānamabhigāyatādbahavo vai me bhaviṣyantīti

word_meaning: Kauṣītakiḥ ha putram uvāca, Kauṣītaki said to his son; aham u etam eva abhyagāsiṣam, I worshipped this [prāṇa] as one; tasmāt, that is why; tvam mama ekaḥ, you are my only son; tvam prāṇān bhūmānam abhigāyatāt, you should worship prāṇa as many [i.e., with manifold qualities and forms]; me bahavaḥ vai bhaviṣyanti iti, thinking, ‘May my children be many.’
commentary: The sun and its rays are not separate, but if a person wants more than one child, he or she will have to worship the sun and its rays as separate entities. The same applies to the worship of the chief prāṇa and its subsidiaries ( vyāna, udāna, etc.).
contextual_topics: The Unitary World-Self, The Immanent Reality of All Things and Man

sanskrit: अथ खलु य उद्गीथः स प्रणवो यः प्रणवः स उद्गीथ इति होतृषदनाद्धैवापि दुरुद्गीथमनुसमाहरतीत्यनुसमाहरतीति
transliteration: atha khalu ya udgīthaḥ sa praṇavo yaḥ praṇavaḥ sa udgītha iti hotṛṣadanāddhaivāpi durudgīthamanusamāharatītyanusamāharatīti
translation: For certain, that which is udgītha is praṇava, and that which is praṇava is also udgītha. Should the person performing a sacrifice make mistakes in pronunciation, that can be rectified [when he has the knowledge that udgītha and praṇava are the same].
word_meaning: Atha khalu, for certain; yaḥ udgīthaḥ saḥ praṇavaḥ, that which is udgītha is praṇava; yaḥ praṇava saḥ udgīthaḥ, that which is praṇava is also udgītha; hotṛṣadanāt api eva ha durudgītam, it is not unlikely that the person performing a sacrifice will err in pronunciation; anusamāharati iti, that can be rectified [the statement is repeated to emphasize its importance].
commentary: It has already been stressed that praṇava and udgītha should be regarded as one. sanskrit: इयमेवर्गग्निः साम तदेतदेतस्यामृच्यध्यूढ़ं साम तस्मादृच्यध्यूढंसाम गीयत इयमेव साग्निरमस्तत्साम
transliteration: iyamevargagniḥ sāma tadetadetasyāmṛcyadhyūḍha़ṃ sāma tasmādṛcyadhyūḍhaṃsāma gīyata iyameva sāgniramastatsāma
translation: This earth is like the Ṛg Veda, and fire is like the Sāma Veda . The Sāma is based on the Ṛg Veda, and this is why the Sāṃa is sung based on the Ṛg Veda. The earth is sā and fire is ama . This sā and ama together make Sāma .
word_meaning: Iyam, this [earth]; eva ṛk, is like the Ṛg Veda; agniḥ sāma, fire is like the Sāma Veda; tat etat sāma etasyām ṛci adhyūḍham, the Sāma Veda is based on the Ṛg Veda; tasmāt, therefore; ṛci adhyūḍham sāma gīyate, the Sāma Veda is sung based on the Ṛg Veda; iyam eva sā, this [earth] is the sā [of Sāma]; agniḥ amaḥ, fire is ama [of Sāma]; tat sāma, that [if joined together] is Sāma [i.e., sā + ama].

contextual_topics: The Unitary World-Self, The Immanent Reality of All Things and Man

transliteration: antarikṣamevargvāyuḥ sāma tadetadetasyāmṛcyadhyūḍhaṃ sāma tasmādṛcyadhyūḍhaṃ sāma gīyate'ntarikṣameva sā vāyuramastatsāma

sanskrit: द्यौरेवर्गादित्यः साम तदेतदेतस्यामृच्यध्यूढं साम तस्मादृच्यध्यूढं साम गीयते द्यौरेव सादित्योऽमस्तत्साम

sanskrit: नक्षत्रान्येवर्क्चन्द्रमाः साम तदेतदेतस्यामृच्यध्यूढं साम तस्मादृच्यध्यूढं साम गीयते नक्षत्राण्येव सा चन्द्रमा अमस्तत्साम

sanskrit: अथ यदेवैतदादित्यस्य शुक्लं भाः सैव साथ यन्नीलं परः कृष्णं तदमस्तत्सामाथ य एषोऽन्तरादित्ये हिरण्मयः पुरुषो दृश्यते हिरण्यश्मश्रुर्हिरण्यकेश आप्रणस्वात्सर्व एव सुवर्णः
transliteration: atha yadevaitadādityasya śuklaṃ bhāḥ saiva sātha yannīlaṃ paraḥ kṛṣṇaṃ tadamastatsāmātha ya eṣo'ntarāditye hiraṇmayaḥ puruṣo dṛśyate hiraṇyaśmaśrurhiraṇyakeśa āpraṇasvātsarva eva suvarṇaḥ
translation: Then, [worship of the effulgent being in the sun]: The white glow of the sun is sā, and the dark bluish-black glow is ama . These two together make up the word Sāma . There is a deity within the orb of the sun, who is seen by yogīs . His whole body glitters like gold, even to his toe-nails. He has a bright golden beard and bright golden hair.
word_meaning: Atha, then; yat eva etat ādityasya śuklam bhāḥ, that which is this white glow of the sun; sā eva sā, that is the ‘sā’ [of Sāma]; atha yat nīlam paraḥ kṛṣṇam, and that which is the deep black glow; tat amaḥ, that is ‘ama’; tat sāma, [when they are put together] that is Sāma; atha antarāditye, again inside the orb of the sun; yāḥ eṣaḥ hiraṇmayaḥ, there is a bright figure; hiraṇyaśmaśruḥ, bright gold beard; hiraṇyakeśaḥ puruṣaḥ dṛśyate, the person with bright gold hair seen [by the yogīs]; āpraṇakhāt sarva eva suvarṇaḥ, bright gold all over the body, including even his nails.
commentary: The sun is partly white and partly dark. sanskrit: तस्य यथा कप्यासं पुण्डरीकमेवमक्षिणी तस्योदिति नाम स एष सर्वेभ्यः पाप्मभ्य उदित उदेति ह वै सर्वेभ्यः पाप्मभ्यो य एवं वेद
transliteration: tasya yathā kapyāsaṃ puṇḍarīkamevamakṣiṇī tasyoditi nāma sa eṣa sarvebhyaḥ pāpmabhya udita udeti ha vai sarvebhyaḥ pāpmabhyo ya evaṃ veda
translation: His eyes are like lotuses blossomed by the sun. He is called ut because he is above all weakness. He who knows this truth is also above all weakness.
word_meaning: Tasya, his; yathā, like; kapyāsam [ kapi, which means ‘he who drinks water’ (i.e, the sun) + āsa, which means blossomed], blossomed by the sun; puṇḍarīkam evam, like the lotus; akṣinī the eyes; tasya ut iti nāma, his name is ‘ut’; saḥ eṣaḥ sarvebhyaḥ pāpmabhyaḥ uditaḥ, he is above all weakness; udeti, he rises; ha vai sarvebhyaḥ pāpmabhyaḥ, above all weakness; yaḥ, who; evam veda, knows thus.
commentary: It has been said that fire rests on the earth, space rests on air, the moon on the stars, and the dark glow of the sun on its white glow. But the Being in the orbit of the sun does not rest on anything He is above all that is evil, above everything. To signify this he is given the name ut (that which is above everything). This ‘ut’ suggests supremacy. It is the kind of supremacy which Vedānta attributes to Brahman . This ‘ut’ and Brahman are the same. Here, Rāmānuja ’s interpretation has been followed for the word kāpyāsam . Śaṅkara gives another interpretation.
contextual_topics: The Individual Self Identical with the Infinite Brahman
claim_candidates: The entity named ut is identified with the supreme Brahman that transcends all weakness
The comparison of the eyes to lotuses blossomed by the sun portrays the luminous and self‑revealing nature of Brahman
The commentary that Brahman rests on nothing indicates its self‑sustaining, independent existence
The designation ut as above all weakness implies that Brahman is superior to all forms of evil
objection_hooks: The term weakness may not be synonymous with evil, so equating being above weakness with being above evil requires clarification
The lotus‑eye metaphor could be a poetic description of beauty rather than an ontological statement about Brahman
The claim that Brahman rests on nothing appears to contradict Upanishadic passages that describe Brahman as pervading all elements

sanskrit: तस्यर्क्च साम च गेष्णौ तस्मादुद्गीथस्तस्मात्त्वेवोद्गातैतस्य हि गाता स एष ये चामुष्मात्पराञ्चो लोकास्तेषां चेष्टे देवकामानां चेत्यधिदैवतम्
transliteration: tasyarkca sāma ca geṣṇau tasmādudgīthastasmāttvevodgātaitasya hi gātā sa eṣa ye cāmuṣmātparāñco lokāsteṣāṃ ceṣṭe devakāmānāṃ cetyadhidaivatam
translation: The Ṛk and the Sāma are his two singers who sing in praise of this god. This is why he is called udgītha, and this is why a singer of the udgītha is called an udgātā . There are worlds above the solar region, but the god in the solar region rules over them [and also supports them]. He also decides the wishes of the gods and goddesses. This is from the standpoint of the gods and goddesses.
word_meaning: Tasya, his; ṛk ca sāma ca geṣṇau, the Ṛk and the Sāma are two singers [who sing his praise]; tasmāt, this is why; udgīthaḥ, he is [called] udgītha [the great God in whose praise songs are sung]; tasmāt, this is why; etasya hi gātā, the singers of it; tu eva udgātā, are called udgātā, the musicians; sāḥ eṣaḥ, he; ye ca, who; amuṣmāt parāñcaḥ, high above that [solar region]; teṣām lokāḥ, those worlds; ca iṣṭe, governs [decides]; devakāmānām ca, the desires
commentary: The word ut suggests supremacy. It is applied to that being who is the overlord of everything and also the source of everything—the earth, the- air, and fire; the Ṛk and Sāma; the gods and goddesses; and even the worlds above the sun. This ‘ut’ rules everything and is therefore identical with Brahman .
contextual_topics: The Individual Self Identical with the Infinite Brahman
claim_candidates: The Ṛk and Sāma function as divine singers, indicating that sacred hymns are the primary means of praising the supreme deity.
The deity called udgītha, who is praised by these hymns, is the overlord of the solar region and also governs the worlds above it.
The supreme deity decides the wishes of other gods and goddesses, implying that even divine beings are subject to his authority.
Because this deity is the source and ruler of all realms, he is identified with Brahman, the ultimate reality.
objection_hooks: How can the Ṛk and Sāma, as textual compositions, be considered literal singers rather than metaphorical representations of devotion?
If the deity governs worlds above the solar region, does this not imply a hierarchy of deities rather than a singular Brahman, challenging the claim of ultimate unity?
The identification of the deity with Brahman may rely on interpretive commentary; is there explicit scriptural evidence within the verse itself to support this equivalence?

sanskrit: अथाध्यात्मं वागेवर्क्प्राणः साम तदेतदेतस्यामृच्यध्यूढं साम तस्मादृच्यध्यूढंसाम गीयते। वागेव सा प्राणोऽमस्तत्साम
transliteration: athādhyātmaṃ vāgevarkprāṇaḥ sāma tadetadetasyāmṛcyadhyūḍhaṃ sāma tasmādṛcyadhyūḍhaṃsāma gīyate| vāgeva sā prāṇo'mastatsāma
translation: Now an explanation with reference to the body: Speech is Ṛk, and prāṇa is Sāma . This Sāma [called prāṇa] is based on the Ṛk [called speech]. This is why Sāma scholars sing songs based on the Ṛk. Speech is sā, and prāṇa is ama . Together they are Sāma.
word_meaning: Atha adhyātmam, now what relates to the body; vāk eva ṛk, speech is Ṛk; prāṇaḥ sāma, prāṇa is Sāma; tat etat sāma, this Sāma [called prāṇa]; etasyām ṛci adhyūdham, is based on Ṛk [speech]; tasmāt, this is why; ṛci adhyūḍham sāma gīyate, the Sāma is sung as based on the Ṛk; vāk eva sā, speech is sā; prāṇaḥ amaḥ, prāṇa is ama; tat sāma, that [if joined together] is Sāma.
commentary: The word prāṇa means both the vital breath and the organ by which we smell. Physically, the organ of speech is below the organ of smell. Similarly, Sāma is known to be based on the Ṛk. In view of their respective positions, Ṛk is equated with speech, and Sāma is equated with prāṇa.
contextual_topics: The Unitary World-Self, The Immanent Reality of All Things and Man
claim_candidates: Speech (vāk) is identified with the Vedic hymn Ṛk in the verse.
Prāṇa (vital breath) is identified with the chant Sāma in the verse.
The chant Sāma is said to be based on the hymn Ṛk, implying a hierarchical dependence of Sāma on Ṛk.
The combination of speech (sā) and prāṇa (ama) yields Sāma, suggesting a synthesis of verbal and vital forces.
The physical ordering of the speech organ below the smell organ is presented as an analogy for the conceptual ordering of Ṛk and Sāma.
objection_hooks: How can speech be equated specifically with the hymn Ṛk rather than with language or sound in general?
Does identifying prāṇa with the particular chant Sāma reduce the universal nature of the vital breath to a specific musical form?
The claim that Sāma is based on Ṛk may overlook the independent sanctity and function of Sāma as a distinct Vedic category.
The analogy of organ placement may be metaphorical and not sufficient to establish ontological identity between Ṛk and Sāma.

sanskrit: अथ यदेतदक्ष्णः शुक्लं भाः सैवर्गथ यन्नीलं परः कृष्णं तत्साम तदेतदेतस्यामृच्यध्यूढंसाम तस्मादृच्यध्यूढंसाम गीयते । अथ यदेवैतदक्ष्णः शुक्लं भाः सैव साथ यन्नीलं परः कृष्णं तदमस्तत्साम
transliteration: atha yadetadakṣṇaḥ śuklaṃ bhāḥ saivargatha yannīlaṃ paraḥ kṛṣṇaṃ tatsāma tadetadetasyāmṛcyadhyūḍhaṃsāma tasmādṛcyadhyūḍhaṃsāma gīyate | atha yadevaitadakṣṇaḥ śuklaṃ bhāḥ saiva sātha yannīlaṃ paraḥ kṛṣṇaṃ tadamastatsāma
translation: Further, there is a white glow in the eyes, and this is compared with the Ṛg Veda . Then there is a similar glow which is a deep, dark blue. This is compared to the Sāma Veda . This dark glow is based on the white glow. This is why the Sāma is said to be based on the Ṛk. Sā of Sāma stands for the white glow in the eye, and ama stands for the deep blue glow. These two together are Sāma.
word_meaning: Atha, then; akṣṇaḥ yat etat śuklam bhaḥ, that which is the white glow in the eyes; saḥ eva ṛk, that is the Ṛg Veda; atha yat nīlam paraḥ kṛṣṇam, then that which is blue and very dark; tat sāma, that is the Sāma; tat etat sāma, this Sāma; etasyām ṛci adhyūḍham, is based on the Ṛk; tasmāt, this is why; ṛci adhyūḍham sāma gīyate, the Sāma is sung as based on the Ṛk; atha yat eva etat akṣṇaḥ śuklam bhāḥ, then this white glow in the eye; sā eva sā, that is sā; atha yat nīlam paraḥ kṛṣṇam, and that which is blue and very dark; tat amaḥ, that is ama; tat sāma, that [if joined together] is Sāma.
commentary: The sun is the support of the power of vision, because without the sun we cannot see. Similarly, the deep blue glow, which is identified with the Sāma, is supported by the white glow, which is the Ṛk.
